title: 'Nuclear Makes It Happen' and 'Electricity Demand Is Now Surging'
claim: Data center electricity use "expected to double by 2030" globally and "triple" in the US; nuclear is "the only source that's both clean and reliable"; AI spot: nuclear powers "billions of devices"
evidence: Primary (Google Ads Transparency + YouTube + Meta Ad Library)
notes: Nuclear industry trade group. 75 Google ads since Jul 2024 (53 video), still running in Oct 2026. Earlier Meta ads (2023–24) boosted coverage of Microsoft's interest in nuclear for AI data centers.
paid_for_by: Nuclear Energy Institute (verified Google advertiser; Meta disclaimer)
audience_who: National YouTube and Google viewers; Meta audience not published for these ads
factcheck_note: The IEA projects global data-center electricity use to more than double by 2030, which matches the ad. For the US, DOE/LBNL projects use to 'double or triple' by 2028, so 'triple' is the top of the range. 'The only source that's both clean and reliable' leaves out hydro and geothermal.

title: Nuclear for AI and data centers
claim: "Investments in nuclear energy are powering America's data centers, meeting AI's growing demands"
notes: Pro-nuclear advocacy campaign. A second ad pitches nuclear careers as AI drives energy demand.
funding_disclosed: Partly: group named, funders not disclosed
factcheck_note: Some data centers buy power from existing nuclear plants, but most announced nuclear-for-data-center deals depend on restarts or new reactors not yet online; the IEA expects the first small modular reactors around 2030.

format: YouTube / Google video ads (incl. 'Clean Jobs for Pennsylvania' channel)
title: 'We Bring The Energy' and Three Mile Island restart spots
claim: "Nation's largest producer of clean and reliable American-made energy", powering "the biggest data centers" with "emissions free electricity"
notes: About 33 Google ads across four Constellation accounts. One account also pays for a 'Clean Jobs for Pennsylvania' channel featuring Three Mile Island workers; those spots don't mention that the Crane restart will supply Microsoft data centers.
funding_disclosed: Partly: some spots run on a 'Clean Jobs for Pennsylvania' channel paid for by Constellation
factcheck_note: Constellation bought Calpine in January 2026, adding over 50 natural-gas plants. 'Emissions free' describes its nuclear fleet, not all of its generation; the spots kept running after the deal.

title: Natural gas for data centers
claim: "Data centers need power 24/7 and natural gas is the most reliable source for that energy"; "Natural gas is America's affordability superpower"
evidence: Primary (Meta Ad Library + Google Ads Transparency)
notes: Interstate gas-pipeline company. Meta issue ads boost CEO interviews tying data center and AI demand to gas. 100+ Google ads (Feb 2025 – Feb 2026), including 30-second brand spots on YouTube with 1.5M+ views each that pitch 'clean natural gas' without naming data centers. A Sep 2026 Ohio ad cites a Cato Institute analysis of its on-site 'Socrates' power project.
paid_for_by: Williams Companies, Inc. (Meta disclaimer; verified Google advertiser)
factcheck_note: Gas plants made up most of the capacity that failed in recent winter storms: 56% in Winter Storm Uri (2021) and 63% in Winter Storm Elliott (2022), per the Union of Concerned Scientists using FERC/NERC data. Gas supply can freeze off when demand peaks.

title: 'Win the AI race' with coal, oil and gas
claim: The US "cannot win the AI race with energy that only works when the wind blows"; "Coal keeps utility bills down!"
notes: American Energy Institute's 'Energy 101' series (600K–700K impressions) and a West Virginia candidate's ad calling to fire coal plants back up. Both use AI and data center demand as the reason.
paid_for_by: American Energy Institute; Brian Helton for West Virginia (Meta disclaimers)
funding_disclosed: Partly: groups named, funders not disclosed
factcheck_note: Studies disagree. Energy Innovation's Coal Cost Crossover (2023) finds 99% of US coal plants cost more to run than replacement with new local wind, solar and storage; an Energy Ventures Analysis study (2025) argues replacing retiring coal plants would cost more. Keeping retiring plants open by federal order has been estimated to cost ratepayers over $3B a year.

title: 'Strengthening Louisiana' / 100 Plan
claim: "Creating 100,000 jobs for Louisiana families—while delivering $2.8B in customer bill savings from data centers"
notes: Utility building seven gas plants for Meta's Hyperion campus. The ad runs without a political-issue label, so Meta publishes no payer, spend or audience. Gas-plant cost figures were redacted in the rate case (see Internal documents, ID-13).
paid_for_by: Not shown: ran without an issue-ad label, so Meta publishes no payer, spend or audience
factcheck_note: Entergy's own 20-year projection (about $650M plus $2B from the Meta deals), which depends on Meta's rates exceeding the cost of serving it. Consumer advocates say the savings rest on optimistic assumptions, and gas-plant costs were redacted in the rate case (Internal documents, ID-13).

format: Facebook/Instagram image and video ads + YouTube
title: 'Do you trust China with your data?'
claim: "Texas data centers keep American data in American hands"; keep data "out of the hands of hostile foreign nations like China"
notes: Since Sep 9, 2026: seven China and national-security Meta ads, six trades-jobs ads and one 'Texas Standard' ad, about $970K–$1.16M combined (Meta ranges), the largest Meta spender in this archive. Earlier YouTube spots were titled 'Data Centers Protect America's National Security'.
paid_for_by: Texans for Economic Liberty (Meta disclaimer; contact at Harris Media LLC)
funding_disclosed: Partly: group named, funders not disclosed
factcheck_note: Implies the alternative to building in Texas is data going to China. Epoch AI estimates the US already hosts about three-quarters of global AI computing capacity and China about 15%; where data is stored depends on company and federal rules, not one state's permits.

title: 'China Is Investing Trillions'
claim: "China is investing trillions to win the tech race"; building data centers will "strengthen national security"
notes: Tech trade association (members include Meta, Google and Amazon). The national ad names Bernie Sanders and AOC; a South Dakota ad reached over 1M impressions. Two placements of the China ad.
funding_disclosed: Partly: trade group named; member companies not shown in the ad
factcheck_note: No source is given for China 'investing trillions'. Epoch AI estimates the US hosts about three-quarters of global AI computing capacity and China about 15%.

title: 'America's Data Center Buildout Is Strengthening Local Communities'
claim: "Data centers create jobs, benefit local communities, and ensure America wins"
evidence: Primary (Meta Ad Library + Google Ads Transparency)
notes: Tech advocacy group that frames tech policy as competition with China. CNBC (May 2023) reported Facebook, now Meta, was its main donor ($34M in 2020–21), so these ads come from a group funded by a company building data centers. Eight Meta ad placements (Sep–Oct 2026), each over 1M impressions ($6K–$20K each).
paid_for_by: American Edge (Meta disclaimer; verified Google advertiser)
funding_disclosed: Partly: group named; donors not disclosed, but CNBC reported Facebook (now Meta) gave $34M in 2020–21 after a $4M seed grant
factcheck_note: Says data centers create jobs without a number, place or time period. Permanent staffing at a data center is usually small; most jobs are temporary construction work.

title: 'Jobs supported' ads
claim: Data centers are "supporting 84,000 jobs" (Ohio), "more than 29,000" (Indiana), "more than 65,000" (Oregon); every data center job "supports 3.5 additional jobs" (Virginia)
notes: Each ad cost $15K–$35K and reached over 1M impressions. The figures match PwC's model for the Data Center Coalition (direct + indirect + induced jobs), not jobs inside data centers. The same groups also ran unlabeled 'tax revenue' ads (Sep–Oct 2026) in seven states.
paid_for_by: America Connects (Data Center Coalition's state-campaign nonprofit); Meta disclaimers name each state group
funding_disclosed: Partly: the ad shows only the state group's name; the industry funder appears only in ad libraries
factcheck_note: These are modeled totals from PwC's study for the Data Center Coalition: direct jobs plus 'indirect and induced' jobs estimated with an economic multiplier, not jobs inside data centers. Facilities themselves employ few permanent staff (often 30–50, up to a few hundred), and Good Jobs First puts the average subsidy in large deals near $2M per job. Georgia's state auditor cut its own data center job estimate by about two-thirds (see Internal documents, ID-17).

title: Saline Township ('The Barn', for Oracle/OpenAI): 'Our Commitment to Michigan'
claim: "Will pay for 100% of its energy costs, so your bills don't go up"; grid investments "will result in $300 million in annual savings for customers"; closed-loop air cooling "saves hundreds of millions of gallons of water"
evidence: Primary (Meta Ad Library + Google Ads Transparency + YouTube)
notes: Developer of the 1.4 GW Saline Township campus built for Oracle (with OpenAI), powered by DTE. 30 Meta ads (several over 1M impressions, $9K–$15K each) and 59 Google video ads; its YouTube spots have 1.8M–5.2M views each. Michigan's Attorney General appealed the regulators' approval of the DTE contracts.
paid_for_by: Related Companies / Related Digital (Meta disclaimers; verified Google advertisers)
funding_disclosed: Yes: developer named; the end user (Oracle) is not named in the ads
factcheck_note: The $300M a year is DTE's own projection of what Oracle's payments will add to fixed grid costs. Michigan regulators approved the contracts with conditions, including that DTE absorbs any shortfall; the Attorney General appealed, and critics say the cost of serving the site could offset the savings.

title: CyrusOne Sangamon County data center
claim: Water use "comparable to 15 new homes"; closed-loop cooling "won't require ongoing water consumption"; "nearly $6 million annually in local property taxes"
notes: Local economic-development group promoting CyrusOne's project. Several ads ran without an issue-ad label.
paid_for_by: Springfield Sangamon Growth Alliance (Meta disclaimer on labeled ads)
funding_disclosed: Partly: some ads unlabeled; CyrusOne named in the ads
factcheck_note: 'Zero water for cooling' covers on-site cooling only. Closed loops still need an initial fill and top-ups, and the water used to generate the electricity can exceed direct use.

sponsor: Southwestern Illinois Coalition for Job Growth
title: 'Data center myths'
claim: "Nationally, golf courses use more water than data centers do on site"; "New data centers use closed-loop recycling"; a large data center "employs more than 100 full-time workers and supports 150 to 400 more jobs"
notes: Building-trades group; ads cite Granite City's closed-loop cooling requirement.
appears_as: Southwestern Illinois Coalition for Job Growth
paid_for_by: Southwestern Illinois Coalition for Job Growth (Meta disclaimer)
funding_disclosed: Partly: coalition named, members not listed in the ads
factcheck_note: Compares only on-site water. National golf-course and data-center totals are not published on the same basis, and on-site figures leave out the water used to generate a data center's electricity. HARC estimates Texas data centers used about 0.4% of state water in 2025, rising to as much as 2.7% by 2030.

title: 'Clean Data Centers' support schools and lower taxes
claim: "Misinformation has been spreading"; today's data centers "use advanced technology to reduce water consumption", "create high paying local jobs" and "generate millions in local tax revenue"
evidence: Primary (Meta Ad Library + Google Ads Transparency)
notes: Pro-data-center group active during Frederick County's data center fight. Funders not disclosed.
paid_for_by: Future Ready Frederick (Meta disclaimer; verified Google advertiser)
funding_disclosed: Partly: group named, funders not disclosed
factcheck_note: Too vague to test (no figure, place or time period).

title: 'Data centers are now required to pay their way'
claim: "Oklahomans wanted assurances data centers wouldn't impact ratepayers - now the law ensures they won't"
notes: Ten ads, all without an issue-ad label, so Meta shows no payer, spend or audience.
paid_for_by: Not shown: ads ran without an issue-ad label
factcheck_note: Oklahoma's Data Center Consumer Ratepayer Protection Act (HB 2992, in force July 1, 2026) requires loads of 75 MW or more to pay for the infrastructure they need. It is new and untested; 'ensures' goes beyond what any rate case has yet shown.

title: Resident testimonials
claim: "Northwest Indiana data centers create new jobs that keep the next generation here"; a site "generating millions to fund housing projects"
notes: Most ads ran without an issue-ad label. One features a Loudoun County, Virginia resident.
paid_for_by: Not shown on most ads (no issue-ad label)
factcheck_note: Says data centers create jobs without a number, place or time period. Permanent staffing at a data center is usually small; most jobs are temporary construction work.

title: Meta DeKalb property taxes
claim: "In 2024 Meta's Dekalb Data Center paid 32.1 million in property taxes"
notes: Electricians' union local.
paid_for_by: Not shown: ad ran without an issue-ad label
factcheck_note: Local reporting gives a $31.1 million property-tax bill for Meta's DeKalb campus (2025). The campus also has a 20-year, 55% property-tax abatement and state sales-tax exemptions.

sponsor: Edison Electric Institute ('We Stand For Energy')
title: Data centers 'put downward pressure on electric rates'
claim: Large data centers "help put downward pressure on electric rates" by "spreading system costs across a broader base"; Missouri law requires them "to pay their fair share"
evidence: Primary (Meta Ad Library + Google Ads Transparency)
notes: Trade association of investor-owned electric utilities, running ads on its 'We Stand For Energy' page. Its 63 Google ads in 2026 are mostly general grid and lineworker spots.
paid_for_by: EEI (Meta disclaimer on its 'We Stand For Energy' page; verified Google advertiser)
funding_disclosed: Partly: page name differs from the payer
factcheck_note: Spreading fixed costs over more sales can lower rates only if a large customer pays more than the new costs it causes. In PJM, the independent market monitor found data center demand added about $9.3B to capacity costs paid by all customers.

title: 'Bloom Energy for Data Centers - Onsite Power for Data Centers'
claim: "Onsite Power for Data Centers"; "Renewable Energy Microgrids"; fuel cells that "Lower Emissions. Move Towards Zero Carbon"; "Generate onsite electricity without combustion using natural gas, biogas or hydrogen"
verbatim: Verbatim (Google Ads Transparency ad previews, read Oct 30, 2026)
notes: Fuel-cell maker whose servers power data centers including Oracle's Project Jupiter plan and Equinix sites. 36 Google ads, mostly search text ads; no data-center Meta ads found.
factcheck_note: 'Without combustion' is accurate, but most Bloom servers run on natural gas. Bloom's own range is 679–833 lb of CO2 per MWh, about the US grid average. 'Renewable' applies only when they run on biogas or hydrogen; Oregon regulators said gas fuel cells would raise AWS's emissions there.

title: 'Water use is a fair question'
claim: "Using dry air cooling in a closed loop… there's no added pressure on local water resources"
notes: Hyperscale operator owned by Blackstone. The ad ran without an issue-ad label.
paid_for_by: Not shown: ad ran without an issue-ad label
factcheck_note: Dry closed-loop cooling avoids evaporative water use on site, but leaves out water used to generate the electricity. AirTrunk has not disclosed water use for its Sydney sites, some of which use adiabatic (evaporative) cooling.

title: Alberta's data centre approach
claim: "Alberta's approach limits data centres to industrial zones, puts them last for water and makes them supply their own power"
notes: Provincial government ad (CA$10K–15K, over 1M impressions). 'Supply their own power' mostly means on-site gas plants.
factcheck_note: Alberta's 'bring your own generation' rule is now law (Data Centre Regulation, June 2026), and most self-supplied power will come from on-site gas plants. We found no rule placing data centres last for water.

title: 'Home ice matters': Bell data centre
claim: Bell's data centre near Regina "will create thousands of good paying jobs" and is "about building to protect Canada's data sovereignty"
notes: The 'data sovereignty' frame parallels US ads about keeping data from China.
factcheck_note: Says data centers create jobs without a number, place or time period. Permanent staffing at a data center is usually small; most jobs are temporary construction work.

title: Counter-ads outside the US
claim: Data centres "competing with [communities] for limited water and energy" (Friends of the Earth, UK); "will guzzle our water" (Environment Centre NT, Australia); "big power bill hikes" (Nova Scotia NDP)
notes: Includes Australian Greens petitions for a data-centre moratorium and Toronto mayoral ads.
paid_for_by: Friends of the Earth, Environment Centre NT, Greens MPs, NSNDP and others (Meta disclaimers)
factcheck_note: Parody or advocacy against data center water use.
